text:
"Now to #Gaza, where the onset of winter poses a severe threat to people who are already so vulnerable.

This is Gaza's fourth winter of war. Just a few days of rain have already flooded camps, destroyed tents and left families exposed to the cold.

A few days ago, an eight-month-old child died of hypothermia.

No child should die from the cold. And winter has barely begun.

An estimated 950,000 displaced people are living in flood-prone areas, including 400,000 at extremely high risk.

For families who have already lost so much, a tent is often their only protection.

When it is gone, they are left exposed to the cold, to contaminated water and to disease.

There are already 33,000 cases of acute respiratory infection – higher than at this time last year.

Flooding is increasing the risk of waterborne diseases.

At the same time, attacks on health care continue, as we saw last week with the attack on the Nasser medical complex.

Damaged health facilities and disrupted transport are making it even harder for people to get care.

We need unobstructed and expedited entry at scale for shelter materials, clean water and sanitation supplies, medicines, vaccines and equipment to prevent hypothermia.

We also need unhindered entry of laboratory supplies that have been denied multiple times, so that disease outbreaks can be detected and responded to early"-@DrTedros

text:
A new study in @BMJOpen_Resp suggests that early-life exposure to #airpollution is linked to poorer lung function 🫁 in childhood, and that the difference persists into adolescence.

Researchers from the University of Copenhagen followed 846 mother-child pairs in the Danish COPSAC2000 and COPSAC2010 cohorts. They modelled exposure to PM2.5 and NO₂ during #pregnancy and the first year of life, and measured lung function from age 3 to 18. Each extra 2 µg/m³ of PM2.5 during pregnancy was associated with nearly 2% lower #lung capacity at age six, and higher exposure was linked to slower lung development through childhood and adolescence.

These effects showed up at relatively low levels. The average annual PM2.5 in the study was 9.6 µg/m³, compared with the @WHO guideline of 5 µg/m³. A

For one child the difference is small, but across a population even small shifts matter for #health. Protecting pregnant women and young children from polluted air is an early investment in lifelong lung health.
